findings.summary: EVERY takeover fixture in this commit is DEPTH ONE (predecessor -> successor). Nothing pins that the successor's OWN checkpoint re-emits the inherited slot WITH ITS POINTER, so the pointer can be dropped on the way through and the whole 319-test module stays green. Surviving mutation, applied and measured in my tree: in CheckpointWriter.inherit (CheckpointWriter.java:96-98) replace `pods.putAll(inherited);` with `inherited.forEach((p, s) -> pods.put(p, Checkpoint.PodState.bare(s.lastAppliedFlushSeq())));` -- BUILD SUCCESSFUL, 319 tests, 0 failed. The backlog notes demand depth two for CheckpointWriter's incarnation-aware merge for exactly this reason; the crossing/pointer fold this row ADDS is only ever exercised at depth one.
findings.failure_scenario: Measured, not argued. I added a probe driving three consecutive leaders -- poda commits (podx, i1, flushSeq 7) at offset 0; podb takes over, commits an unrelated pod's flush so it writes its own checkpoint; podc takes over and receives a replay of the SAME (podx, i1, 7) triple. Unmutated production answers correctly: `PROBE depth2 assigned=0 replayOffset=0`. Under the pointer-dropping mutation above the same probe prints `PROBE depth2 assigned=0 replayOffset=4` -- the replay is COMMITTED A SECOND TIME, the same records get a second set of offsets, and I2 is violated. That is precisely the defect M4.10d exists to prevent, and the suite reports it as passing. Mechanism: bare slots have `incarnationId == null`, so `LocalSequencer.inherit`'s guard skips them, and the third leader's window is empty for podx. Remedy: one depth-two fixture in SequencerDedupTest that takes over twice and asserts the replay is still answered at its ORIGINAL offsets.

findings.summary: The new argued-equivalent entry for `IdempotencyWindow.applied`'s `flushSeq > prior.lastAppliedFlushSeq()` boundary rests on a premise that is FALSE. It says: "`applied` is reached only for submissions `replayOf` called FRESH -- which is `flushSeq > lastApplied` by construction, so the equal case cannot arrive." The equal case DOES arrive. `LocalSequencer.commitAll` classifies EVERY request in the batch against the window BEFORE any of them is recorded, so two requests in one batch carrying the same (podId, incarnationId, flushSeq) are both classified fresh, and the second `applied(...)` call in `applyFresh`'s loop hits `request.flushSeq() == prior.lastAppliedFlushSeq()`. The mutant is still equivalent, but for a DIFFERENT reason the entry does not state: every request inside one `applyFresh` call is recorded with the same `log.epoch()` and `delta.sequence()`, so the replacement `Applied` record is field-for-field identical to the one it replaces.
findings.failure_scenario: Measured, not argued. I inserted `if (prior != null && request.flushSeq() == prior.lastAppliedFlushSeq()) throw new IllegalStateException("EQUAL CASE REACHED via commitAll")` into `IdempotencyWindow.applied` and drove `sequencer.commitAll(List.of(new CommitRequest("poda","i1",5,"seg/a",counts(1)), new CommitRequest("poda","i1",5,"seg/b",counts(1))))` through the real LocalSequencer. Output: `PROBE EQUAL CASE REACHED via commitAll`. I separately confirmed the mutant survives the module (`>` -> `>=`: BUILD SUCCESSFUL, 319 tests, 0 failed). The consequence: this baseline entry suppresses a PIT mutant on a stated reason a future reader will check and find true-looking. The moment `applied` is called with a per-request pointer -- a batch split across two deltas, a per-segment sequence, anything M4.9's bounded recovery might bring -- the equal case starts writing a DIFFERENT `Applied`, the mutant stops being equivalent, and the entry keeps suppressing it silently while its justification still reads as sound. Remedy: either rewrite the entry to the argument that is actually true (one `applyFresh`, one `(epoch, sequence)`, so the equal case rewrites an identical record) or drop the entry and kill the mutant with a two-identical-triples-in-one-batch test.

findings.summary: In `theSuccESSORSFirstCheckpointCarriesThePredecessorsPodsThroughSTART` the fixture commits `flushSeq 0`, so the second assertion `assertThat(written.pods().get("podx").lastAppliedFlushSeq()).as("at the watermark the predecessor recorded").isEqualTo(0L)` cannot distinguish the inherited watermark from a reset one -- 0 is both the recorded value and the reset value. Surviving mutation: `CheckpointWriter.inherit` -> `inherited.forEach((p, s) -> pods.put(p, new Checkpoint.PodState(s.incarnationId(), 0L, s.epoch(), s.sequence())));` leaves this test GREEN (measured: only `CheckpointWriterContentTest#theFirstCheckpointAfterATakeoverCARRIESThePredecessorsPods`, which uses 42, fails).
findings.failure_scenario: A change that adopts a predecessor's pod slots but zeroes their watermarks would pass this test, whose stated purpose is that the wiring works THROUGH `start` -- the sibling test that catches it is the one this test's own javadoc says is 'NOT the test that proves the wiring'. So the through-start path is unpinned on the value, and the value is what stops the successor from re-accepting every flush the predecessor already applied. Remedy: use a non-zero flushSeq in the fixture, as the sibling does.

findings.summary: The two identity halves of `answers()` mask each other: no fixture has one delta holding two segments that share a flushSeq AND one of podId/incarnationId. Surviving mutations, each measured green over the whole module: (a) `&& a.podId().equals(request.podId())` -> `&& true`; (b) `&& a.incarnationId().equals(request.incarnationId())` -> `&& true`. Dropping BOTH is caught (by `aReplayIsAnsweredWithITSOwnSegmentOutOfABatchedDelta`), and dropping the flushSeq comparison is caught, so the field is jointly but not individually constrained.
findings.failure_scenario: The javadoc on `answers()` claims 'THE EXACT TRIPLE'. If podId were dropped, two pods that minted the same incarnationId string (nothing in `CommitRequest` enforces a UUID) and the same flushSeq inside one batched delta would answer each other's retry with the WRONG pod's offsets, and a producer would acknowledge records committed at offsets belonging to another pod. `aReplayIsAnsweredWithITSOwnSegmentOutOfABatchedDelta` already puts two pods in one delta at flushSeq 0; giving them the same incarnationId string, or adding a third case that does, kills (a) and (b) individually.

findings.summary: The bare-slot guard in `LocalSequencer.inherit` has no fixture. Surviving mutation, measured green: `if (slot.incarnationId() != null && slot.hasPointer())` -> `if (true)`. Note also that the two conjuncts are the SAME predicate -- `Checkpoint.PodState.hasPointer()` is literally `return incarnationId != null` -- so nothing in the module ever reaches the false arm and the guard's stated justification ('adopting one would refuse a live pod's next flush while being unable to return the offsets it refused it for') is not what happens: an adopted bare slot keys as `podId + "\0null"` and is simply inert.
findings.failure_scenario: A v0 checkpoint (pre-ADR-0036, still decodable for the retention window per the format comment) yields bare slots, and no test drives one through `inherit`. If the window key format ever changes so that a null incarnationId does NOT produce an unreachable key -- for instance keying on podId alone during a migration -- an adopted bare slot would carry `(epoch, sequence) = (-1, -1)` and every replay it matched would take the `holds no delta` throw instead of being answered. Remedy: one fixture whose predecessor checkpoint carries `Checkpoint.PodState.bare(n)`, asserting the successor accepts that pod's next flush.

findings.summary: Nothing constrains the sequence returned for an all-replay batch spanning more than one delta, nor the sequence returned for a mixed batch. Two surviving mutations, both measured green over the whole module: (a) `sequenceOf`'s `Math.max(...)` -> `Math.min(...)`; (b) in `LocalSequencer.commitAll`, `return new CommitDelta(delta.sequence(), merged);` -> `return new CommitDelta(window.sequenceOf(replays), merged);`. Every fixture replays exactly one triple, or points every replay at one delta, so max and min coincide.
findings.failure_scenario: `aReplayedTripleReturnsTheORIGINALOffsetsAndAppendsNoSecondDelta` asserts `replay.sequence() == first.sequence()` for a single replay, which is the only pin on this value. A batch replaying two triples applied in DIFFERENT deltas returns one sequence that is right for at most one of them, and no test says which it should be -- so the choice is unstated behaviour that a refactor can flip without any test noticing. Note the value also drops the EPOCH: a replay answered across a takeover returns the predecessor's sequence number, which names a different object in the successor's chain, and nothing asserts what a caller may do with it.

findings.summary: `answer()`'s stated cost bound has no test. The javadoc says 'AT MOST ONE GET PER DISTINCT (epoch, sequence), which is the cost bound ADR-0036 states'. Surviving mutation, measured green: `CommitDelta pointed = read.get(slot);` -> `CommitDelta pointed = null;`, which removes the cache and issues one GET per replayed REQUEST. testing.md rule 22 makes cost assertions tests, `RecordingBinStore` is already in this module, and the sibling claim in `LocalSequencer.inherit` ('ZERO ADDITIONAL REQUESTS') IS pinned by the existing exact-cost assertions -- this one is not.
findings.failure_scenario: A batch of N retries from one pod all pointing at the same delta would silently go from 1 GET to N GETs, and the only thing saying that is wrong is a comment. The `store.get` sits inside a `for (CommitRequest request : replays)` loop, which the cost lens treats as a finding until proven otherwise, and the proof here is the cache -- untested. Remedy: one `RecordingBinStore` assertion on the exact GET count for a two-replay batch pointing at one delta.

findings.summary: The fake's dedup gained two arms that the two new FakeSequencerTest cases do not reach. Surviving mutations, both measured green over the whole module: (a) delete `segments.addAll(answered);` -- the fake's MIXED batch (replay + fresh) silently drops the replayed segment from the returned delta, while production's identical line `merged.addAll(answered)` IS killed by `aBatchMixingAReplayWithAFreshFlushCommitsTheFreshOneAndAnswersTheReplay`; (b) `return new CommitDelta(nextSequence - 1, answered);` -> `nextSequence`, while production's counterpart is pinned by `aReplayedTripleReturnsTheORIGINALOffsetsAndAppendsNoSecondDelta` asserting `replay.sequence() == first.sequence()`.
findings.failure_scenario: `Sequencer`'s javadoc now asserts 'FakeSequencer models the refusal', and FakeSequencer is published in testFixtures for other modules to test their retry paths against. The mixed-batch arm and the returned-sequence arm are the two places the fake can diverge from `LocalSequencer` without any test in this module noticing, so a consumer's retry test would be written against behaviour that is unconstrained here. Separately and untested: the fake answers only EXACT triples from a map it never evicts, so the case `aReplayThePointedDeltaDoesNotCarryIsREFUSED` pins as an IOException in production is silently ANSWERED by the fake -- disclosed in a comment, asserted nowhere. Remedy: mirror the mixed-batch and returned-sequence assertions into FakeSequencerTest.
